transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Um, I came in because I'm having a really hard time lately. I just can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. 

I do IT support, so I'm on video calls a lot for work, and I see it constantly there... and also in photos from my salsa classes. It's getting to the point where it's really messing with my job and my social life. The frustrating part is that everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything wrong, or that they don't know what I'm talking about, but I just can't stop fixating on it.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, touching your face, or comparing sides, to try to fix or check how your face looks?

Yeah, I do. Um, a lot, actually. Right before my meetings or if I'm getting ready to go out, I just keep opening the camera preview on my screen. I'll sit there changing the angle and the lighting, or trying to fix my hair so it falls around that side of my face to hide it. 

I also end up taking and retaking pictures of myself over and over just to check how it looks. And... I keep asking my friends if I look strange or uneven. I do it so much that I usually end up running late, or honestly, I just get too drained from doing all of that and decide not to go out at all.

How much does this concern about your face interfere with your daily life—like your work, relationships, or other important areas of functioning? Can you give me an example of how it’s affected you recently?

It interferes a lot, honestly. At work, um, I've actually missed some ticket deadlines because I get so caught up checking my camera. I've joined a few video calls late, too, just trying to fix how I look before logging on. It got to the point where my supervisor actually brought it up during my last performance review, which was really hard to hear. 

And outside of work... well, I mentioned the salsa classes earlier. I've been skipping those nights, and other community events too, especially if I know people are going to be taking photos. I just stay home instead because I can't handle the thought of being in them. So yeah, it's definitely affecting my day-to-day life.

Do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental acts in response to your concerns about your face, like adjusting your appearance, checking yourself in mirrors, or mentally comparing how you look?

Um, yeah, I think that's kind of what I was getting at a minute ago with the camera previews and taking all those pictures. I definitely feel driven to do it. It's like... I can't just open my laptop and start a meeting. I absolutely have to check the lighting and fix my hair first, or I just can't focus on anything else. 

And as for the mental part you mentioned, about comparing... yeah, I do that too. When I'm on those support calls, I'll catch myself looking at the other people on the screen, just checking to see if their faces look uneven or puffy like mine. I just constantly compare how they look to how I look. So, yeah, it's pretty much an urge I can't really ignore.
When you're not focused on checking or adjusting your appearance, how do you generally feel emotionally? Are there other things that have been bothering you lately?

Um, honestly, when I'm actually able to stop focusing on it, I feel mostly fine. My mood is generally okay. I don't think there's really anything else that's been bothering me lately. 

It's really just... this one issue with my face. It takes up so much of my mental energy that it's kind of the only thing causing me stress. If I didn't have to worry about how I looked, I think I'd be doing pretty well. So yeah, outside of that, I don't have any other major emotional stuff going on.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms are primarily centered around a preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (asymmetry/puffiness of the face), repetitive behaviors (checking, camouflaging), and significant impairment in functioning. No other significant emotional or behavioral issues were endorsed. This presentation is most consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (F45.22). Other candidates (F32.3, F43.23) were ruled out due to absence of criteria such as major depressive episodes or significant stressors with adjustment disorder.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation suggests a possible somatic symptom disorder given the patient's preoccupation with a perceived physical defect (uneven and puffy left side of the face). Differential diagnoses include major depressive disorder and adjustment disorder with depressed mood due to the impact on work and social functioning. No definitive exclusion of any disorder yet.
